newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Albacom aims for No 2 spot in Italy telecoms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Albacom aims for No 2 spot in Italy telecoms.

text.p: Italy's telecom venture Albacom set its sights on being the nation's number two operator of fixed line telephony on Thursday after state-controlled oil giant ENI agreed to take a 35 percent stake in the grouping.

ENI brings its national fibre optics network to the Albacom venture, which already includes British Telecommunications Plc, multi-media group Mediaset and state-controlled banking group Banca Nazionale del Lavoro (BNL).

Albacom's aim to be number two operator in Italy after state-controlled Telecom Italia TIT.MI sets it up against Olivetti -led consortium Infostrada which is already gunning for the number two telecom spot in Italy.

After the entry of ENI, BT and BNL will hold 45.5 percent of Albacom through investment vehicle Albacom Holding, while Mediaset will hold the remaining 19.5 percent directly. Albacom Holding is 50.5 percent owned by BT and 49.5 percent by BNL.

In the deal, Albacom will take over the telecoms infrastructure of ENI's natural gas unit Snam, and will draw up a contract with Snam for the use of fibre optic cables. The deal must now be cleared by the European Commission.

Albacom's chairman Giuliano Venturi told a news conference that the venture would invest 1.5 trillion lire ($842 million) in the next 10 years, and 60 percent of this in the first four years, in a bid to become Italy's number two telephone operator.

The battle to become Italy's second fixed line telecom group will depend on the cost and speed of setting up a new fixed-line infrastructure, chosen partners and the volume of traffic it can attract from day one of operation, analysts said.
"Albacom has good rights of way and good partners, but has no cellular phone interest," said telecoms industry analyst Bill Colman at HSBC James Capel in London.

The Olivetti-led Infostrada venture brings in powerful partners France Telecom and Bell Atlantic and it took a further step forward last August when Olivetti and France Telecom agreed to buy a 70 percent stake in Italian state railway Ferrovie dello Stato's domestic phone network.

Olivetti and Bell Atlantic are also the two leading members of Italy's second mobile phone consortium Omnitel which started operations in December 1995 in competition with state-controlled Telecom Italia Mobile.
A mobile link-up can help a new fixed-line network built up traffic by diverting its business onto the fixed-line operator.

However, British Telecom is optimistic about the Italian market set to be liberalised at the start of next year, and a group spokesman said in London that Albacom aimed to win 10-15 percent of the Italian telephone market by 2006/7.
In addition, Albacom's partners have expressed interest in bidding for Italy's third licence to operate the nation's new mobile phone licence scheduled to be issued later this year.
BT's managing director for global communications Alfred Mockett said that he understood that bids for the third mobile licence will be by October for assignment in December.
"We are in discussions with ENI on their participation. We need a mobile dimension to our strategy in Italy," he said.
The only other party to show official interest in the third licence is a venture between Italian electricity utility ENEL and Deutsche Telekom. ($1=1,782 lire)
